title: One-person posts that changed hands with no gap
question: Where the only holder of a job class in a department was replaced during a year, how often do the two people’s paid hours add up to a single full year, and was the newcomer already a City employee?
finding: Between fiscal 2018 and 2025, 20 one-person posts changed hands inside a fiscal year with the outgoing and incoming holders’ paid hours adding to about one full year (1,950 to 2,250 hours), which leaves no room for a vacancy. That is few. In 4 of them the newcomer was not on the City payroll before that year, and none of those was a permanent civil-service appointment, the kind that needs an examination and a list; 3 were exempt appointments. For scale, the civil grand jury put the middle time to fill a City job at 255 days in 2023.
how: City payroll file, fiscal 2017 to 2026. A post is a job class in a department with exactly one paid holder the year before (1,800 hours or more) and exactly one, a different person, the year after (1,800 hours or more), and those same two people in the year between. Listed: posts where the two people’s hours in the class that year total 1,950 to 2,250. The newcomer’s earlier record is read from the payroll by name. Posts filled from outside the payroll come first, permanent civil-service appointments before exempt ones, by rate of pay.
limits: The payroll has no dates: it cannot show when the post was advertised, when an examination was held, whether anyone else applied or how the appointment was made. Those are in the job announcement and appointment records, which this project is still collecting. No gap is what good planning looks like: a retirement announced months ahead lets the recruitment finish before the holder leaves, and an exempt post needs no examination. Paid hours may include leave paid out on departure, which would hide a short vacancy; and a name new to the file may be a former employee from before the file had names.
